description: Table 3 is a plain text table rendered as an image, with a single header row and three data rows, no graphics, colour scales, micrographs or error bars. The two data columns are headed "Model 1(varying conditions)" and "Model 2(varying conditions)"; the row labels down the left side are "RMSE (MPa)", "R²" and "AARE". The cells read: Model 1 — RMSE 6.4554 MPa, R² 0.8239, AARE 7.36 %; Model 2 — RMSE 3.0399 MPa, R² 0.9507, AARE 3.11 %. These are the only printed values; the units are MPa for the error and percent for AARE, while R² is dimensionless. No alloy, temperature or strain-rate labels appear in the table itself, so the "varying conditions" are named only in the column headers. Comparing the two columns, Model 2 is better on every listed metric: its RMSE is roughly half that of Model 1, its AARE is less than half, and its R² is higher. The figure therefore demonstrates that the second constitutive/flow-stress model reproduces measured flow stress more accurately than the first when deformation conditions vary, which the citing text links to improved finite-element load prediction.

observations.observation: Table 3 compares two models in two data columns headed exactly "Model 1(varying conditions)" and "Model 2(varying conditions)", with only three row labels: "RMSE (MPa)", "R²" and "AARE".
Model 1(varying conditions) reports R² = 0.8239 while Model 2(varying conditions) reports R² = 0.9507.
Model 1(varying conditions) reports AARE = 7.36 % while Model 2(varying conditions) reports AARE = 3.11 %.
Model 2 has the better value of every metric in the table: lower RMSE, lower AARE and higher R² than Model 1.
The only units printed in the table are MPa (for RMSE) and percent (for AARE); the table contains no sample identifiers, temperatures, strain rates or other test conditions.
The caption states that Table 3 is the accuracy evaluation of flow stress using both models under varying deformation conditions.
The citing text asserts that compared to Model 1, Model 2 exhibited a higher R² as well as lower RMSE and AARE, indicating superior performance under varying conditions.
The citing text links this table to a finite-element simulation of hot compression under varying deformation conditions compared with experimental results (Fig. 10).

The citing text states that Model 1 delayed forecasting the decline in flow stress following an abrupt decrease in strain rate or a temperature rise (Fig. 8c, 9c), whereas Model 2 better captured force evolution under varying deformation conditions.
The citing text concludes that optimizing t0.5 and characteristic stresses can improve the accuracy of load prediction in the constitutive model.
